title: Interfaces should feel like instruments
summary: The best interfaces do not explain themselves with paragraphs. They give you enough structure to start touching the system and learning its behavior.
body:
I keep coming back to interfaces that feel more like instruments than forms. A good instrument has constraints, feedback, and enough ambiguity that you can discover a way of using it that belongs to you.

That is a lot of what I like about Teenage Engineering products, music software, good games, and the kinds of data interfaces I want to build. The interface is not there to disappear. It is there to give shape to a system without flattening it.

I think this is especially important for AI products. A blank text box is flexible, but it also hides structure. I am more interested in interfaces that let people see the machinery they are working with: sources, states, transformations, alternatives, and consequences.

title: Why provenance is an interface problem
summary: Showing where a number came from should not be a footnote. It should be part of the interaction.
body:
While building Ledgerline, the part I got most interested in was not the charting. It was provenance.

Financial answers are unusually sensitive to context. A number can be technically correct and still be misleading if you do not know the period, filing, accounting concept, or transformation behind it. Most AI interfaces treat citations as decoration at the end of an answer.

I think provenance should behave more like a first-class UI primitive. Click the number. See the period. See the XBRL concept. See the filing. See what changed between the source and the value on screen.

That idea extends well beyond finance. If an AI system is doing meaningful analytical work, the path from evidence to output should be explorable.

title: Blue in Green and the value of leaving space
summary: Some things get stronger when you stop filling every available inch.
body:
Blue in Green is probably my favorite piece of music because almost nothing in it feels wasted.

The harmony is dense, but the arrangement leaves air around it. Notes arrive with enough room for the color of the chord to actually register. The restraint is doing as much work as the playing.

I think about that when I design. There is a temptation to prove that an interface is useful by filling it with controls, cards, labels, suggestions, and status. Usually the thing gets better when half of that disappears.

Density is useful when the information demands it. Otherwise, space is not emptiness. It is part of the hierarchy.

title: Games are very good at teaching systems
summary: A good strategy game can teach a complicated ruleset without ever feeling like a spreadsheet tutorial.
body:
I like games that expose complicated systems gradually and then let you become fluent in them through use.

Fire Emblem is a good example. Positioning, probability, resources, character growth, weapon relationships, and long-term consequences all coexist, but the system becomes legible because every decision has immediate visual feedback.

That is basically an interface-design problem. The player needs enough information to make a meaningful decision, but not so much explanation that the decision stops feeling like theirs.

I want more educational and financial software to borrow from games in that way. Not points and badges. Actual system legibility.

title: I want financial software to show its work
summary: Most finance tools either overwhelm you with terminal-density or hide the model behind a friendly summary.
body:
There is a weird split in financial software. On one end you get professional tools that assume you already understand the system. On the other, consumer products simplify everything until the mechanics disappear.

The interesting middle ground is software that can reveal complexity progressively.

Show me the simple answer first. Then let me open the assumptions. Let me compare periods. Let me trace the input. Let me change the representation. Let me see what the model did.

That is the direction I am increasingly interested in: interfaces that make complicated systems approachable without pretending they are simple.

title: Small public projects beat giant private ideas
summary: Shipping something small changes the way you think about the work.
body:
I have a bad habit of liking the idea of a giant project more than the boring last twenty percent that makes a small project real.

Putting things on a live URL has been a useful correction. Once a project is public, all the little decisions matter: loading states, ugly edge cases, copy, links, deployment, whether another person can understand what the thing is without me standing beside them.

That is a much more useful kind of pressure than endlessly making a prototype more ambitious.

I still like big ideas. I just want to get better at making them out of small finished pieces.
